title: Prepare a Fresh Herb‑Infused Water with Thin Basil Slices
meta_description: Learn how to make refreshing herb‑infused water using thin basil slices with a mandoline. Tips, techniques, and a top mandoline slicer recommendation included.
html:
Infused water is a simple way to stay hydrated while adding a burst of flavor. When you slice basil thin enough to release its essential oils, the result is a bright, aromatic drink that feels like a spa‑day in a glass. Using a mandoline basil slices herb water technique ensures every slice is uniformly thin, so the flavor extracts quickly without turning the water bitter. Below is a step‑by‑step guide that shows how to prep fresh herb‑infused water with restaurant‑thin basil slices, plus a few variations to keep things interesting.

Why Thin Basil Slices Matter

Whole basil leaves tend to float on top of the water and release flavor slowly. When the leaves are cut into thin ribbons, the surface area increases dramatically, allowing the herb’s volatile compounds to mingle with the liquid almost immediately. This means you get a fragrant, mildly sweet infusion in under five minutes instead of waiting an hour. Thin slices also make the drink look polished—perfect for brunch tables or office coolers.

Choosing the Right Tool: Mandoline Slicer

The secret to consistent, restaurant‑thin slices is a quality mandoline. The Mandoline Slicer offers adjustable blades and a safety hand guard, letting you glide basil leaves through with minimal effort. Whether you’re prepping a single batch or scaling up for a party, the mandoline’s precision saves time and eliminates the uneven cuts you get with a knife.

Step‑by‑Step: Preparing Basil‑Infused Water

  1. Gather fresh basil. Choose leaves that are bright green, firm, and free of wilting. Rinse them gently under cool water and pat dry with a paper towel.
  2. Set up your mandoline. Attach the finest blade setting—usually labeled “julienne” or “thin ribbon.” Adjust the hand guard so you can slide the leaves safely.
  3. Slice the basil. Place a handful of leaves on the mandoline platform and slide them back and forth. You’ll collect delicate, translucent ribbons that are about 1 mm thick.
  4. Combine with water. In a pitcher, add 1‑2 cups of cold filtered water for every 10–12 basil ribbons. Stir gently.
  5. Let it sit. Allow the mixture to rest for 3‑5 minutes. The water will take on a subtle green hue and a fresh, aromatic scent.
  6. Serve. Pour the infused water over ice, garnish with a whole basil leaf or a slice of lemon, and enjoy.

Because the basil is sliced so thin, you can taste its flavor almost instantly. If the water tastes too strong, simply add more plain water or a splash of sparkling water for a fizzy twist.

Creative Twists on Basil‑Infused Water

Once you’ve mastered the basic recipe, experiment with complementary ingredients. A few ideas:

  • Citrus boost: Add thin orange or lime slices alongside the basil for a bright, tangy note.
  • Berry burst: Toss in a handful of fresh strawberries or raspberries for a hint of sweetness.
  • Cooling cucumber: Combine cucumber ribbons (also made with a mandoline) for an extra refreshing quality.

These variations keep the drink interesting throughout the week and make it easy to match the flavor profile to the season or your menu.

Tips for Keeping Your Mandoline Safe and Effective

Using a mandoline can feel intimidating at first, but these safety habits will keep you confident:

  • Always engage the hand guard before you start slicing.
  • Never force the blade; let the leaf glide at its own pace.
  • After each use, brush off any food residue and wipe the blade with a damp cloth. This prevents rust and maintains sharpness.
  • Store the mandoline with the blade covered or in a protective case to avoid accidental cuts.

Regular maintenance ensures the mandoline continues to produce the perfect, even slices you need for herb water and other recipes.

When to Serve Basil‑Infused Water

This drink shines as a palate cleanser between courses, a light alternative to soda at summer picnics, or a hydrating option for a work‑from‑home desk. Its subtle flavor pairs well with Mediterranean dishes, grilled chicken, and light salads. Because the infusion is quick, you can prepare it minutes before guests arrive, guaranteeing freshness.

FAQ

Can I use dried basil instead of fresh?

Dried basil won’t produce the same bright, clean flavor and can make the water taste gritty. For the best result, stick with fresh leaves and thin slices.

How long can I keep basil‑infused water in the fridge?

Store it in a sealed pitcher for up to 24 hours. After that, the basil may turn bitter and the color will darken.

Do I need a special blade for herbs?

The standard fine‑julienne blade on the Mandoline Slicer works well for basil. If you prefer even thinner ribbons, many mandolines offer an extra‑fine setting that’s perfect for delicate herbs.
